name: Plan 9 from Bell Labs
summary: Distributed research operating system designed by the original creators of Unix at Bell Labs, unifying all local and remote resources through the 9P protocol and private per-process namespaces.
license: Open Source (MIT Licence / Lucent Public License)

content.introduction: Plan 9 from Bell Labs is a distributed research operating system designed at the end of the 1980s within the prestigious Bell Labs (AT&T / Lucent Technologies) by the very team that had created Unix and the C language: Ken Thompson, Rob Pike, Dennis Ritchie, Dave Presotto, Phil Winterbottom and Tom Duff. The project aimed to go beyond the conceptual limits of Unix by creating a natively distributed computing environment, where computing power (CPU servers), data storage (file servers) and user interaction (graphical terminals) are spread over the network and unified through transparent access semantics.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Plan 9 is neither a derivative of Unix nor a Linux distribution: it is a stand-alone system that reinvents the foundations of Unix by pushing the "everything is a file" principle to its extreme. In Plan 9, every resource — local processes, hardware devices, memory, graphical display, TCP/IP network interfaces and remote servers — is exposed in the form of a hierarchical file tree. Innovatively, Plan 9 eliminates the single global tree: each process has its own private and dynamic namespace, which it composes freely through bind and mount operations allowing directory overlays (union mounts).
content.the_9p_distributed_protocol: The architectural heart and unifying element of Plan 9 is the standardised communication protocol **9P** (also called 9P2000 or Styx). In Plan 9, every operation on a resource (open, read, write, close, query of attributes) translates into 9P messages. This protocol works in a rigorously identical way, whether the resource is local (communication through shared memory or pipes) or hosted on a remote machine across the local network or the Internet. Access to the files, the network stack or the graphical server of a remote machine therefore takes place with the same standard system calls as for local storage, abolishing any artificial boundary between local and distributed computing.
content.kernel_architecture_and_utf8_encoding: The Plan 9 kernel is remarkably compact, modular and elegant. It eliminates many historical complexities of Unix: no complex asynchronous signals (replaced by textual note strings passed to processes), no hard links and fine concurrency management through the `rfork()` system primitive. It is also for Plan 9 that the universal character encoding **UTF-8** was invented in 1992 by Ken Thompson and Rob Pike, and it is used natively and systematically throughout the system, from file names to source code.
content.rio_window_manager_and_acme_environment: The Plan 9 user environment is organised around the **Rio** window manager (successor of 8½). Rio is itself a 9P server: each window created by a user is an isolated environment that exposes its own keyboard input, mouse and matrix display buffer as virtual files, allowing the recursive execution of Rio inside one of its own windows. The ecosystem also includes the structural editor **Sam**, the innovative textual integrated development environment **Acme** (entirely driven by the three-button mouse and turning every word displayed on screen into an executable command), as well as the **rc** shell designed by Tom Duff.
content.licensing_governance_and_legacy: After being distributed under academic research licences by AT&T, then under the Lucent Public License (LPL) and the GNU GPLv2, all the intellectual property rights and the source code of Plan 9 were transferred in 2021 by Bell Labs (Nokia) to the non-profit **Plan 9 Foundation**, which placed them under the free and permissive **MIT Licence**. While the official Bell Labs distribution remains today a heritage and academic study object, its principles continue to live and evolve through active derived projects, in particular the community fork **9front**.
content.distribution_quatrieme_edition_et_suppor: The reference distribution remains the fourth edition of Plan 9, maintained by the Plan 9 Foundation: it contains the source code of the kernel, libraries and commands for all supported architectures, as well as the complete binaries for the x86 architecture. The CD image provided is at once a live bootable CD and an installation CD; the boot menu lets the user choose between exploring the system and installing it, and a USB disk image is also offered. Installation from floppy disk is described as obsolete, the floppy variant omitting several drivers — USB, AHCI, some Ethernet interfaces — to fit the format. The documentation asks the reader to consult the list of supported PC hardware before any installation, as well as the plan9.ini(8) and prep(8) manual pages.
content.security_namespace_isolation_and_capabil: Plan 9 divides access control between authentication and namespace. The library described by `auth(2)` provides `newns`, which rebuilds a namespace for a user from `/lib/namespace`, `addns`, which applies commands to the current namespace, `amount`, which mounts a file system while performing the required authentication, and `login`, which changes the process identifier and then recreates the namespace. `procsetuser` changes the identifier without touching the namespace and only `hostowner` can assign an identifier other than `none`; `noworld` tests membership of the group of the same name in `/adm/users` and serves for the confinement of `telnetd` and `ftpd` sessions. After authentication, the `AuthInfo` structure carries the client and server identities, a `cap` capability usable with the `cap(3)` device to change the identifier of a process, and a shared secret used to derive the session keys. The `factotum(4)` service manages keys and opens a private channel at each `rpc` opening; `securenet(8)` documents a hardware challenge-response token, whose key fits in eight three-digit octal numbers. The pages consulted describe primitives and tools; they set neither a support period nor an advisory register.
advantages: Distributed architectural design of legendary purity and conceptual elegance.
Full generalisation of the "everything is a file" model and private per-process namespaces.
9P protocol transparently unifying local resources and remote network services.
Birthplace of the universal UTF-8 encoding, natively integrated at all levels of the system.
Innovative development environments (Acme, Sam, Rio) offering remarkable textual productivity.
Source code entirely open, documented and governed by the permissive free MIT licence under the aegis of the Plan 9 Foundation.
disadvantages: The official Bell Labs branch is no longer actively maintained on contemporary physical hardware.
Incompatibility with the vast majority of software written for modern POSIX environments without porting.
No support for modern hardware (contemporary Wi-Fi, recent 3D GPUs, NVMe, UEFI on the historical branch).
Demanding learning curve requiring a rethink of working habits forged on classic Unix/Linux systems.
Reserved for academic study, virtual environments or experimentation with distributed systems.
who_is_it_for: Computer science researchers, teachers and students exploring distributed operating system architectures.
Developers and enthusiasts wishing to study the successor of Unix designed by its historical authors.
Programmers appreciating the minimalist and highly productive ergonomics of the Acme textual environment.
Virtualisation enthusiasts wishing to experiment with an unconventional operating system under QEMU.
who_is_it_not_for: General public users looking for a primary desktop system for modern office work or multimedia web.
Enterprises looking for a production server system compatible with Linux containers (Docker, Kubernetes).
Developers depending on modern closed software ecosystems or proprietary 3D graphics drivers.
System administrators looking for strict compliance with standard POSIX/Linux norms.
content.verdict: Plan 9 from Bell Labs is a research operating system developed by Bell Labs. It rests on an architecture unified by files, namespaces and the 9P protocol. Its original branch now belongs to historical study; the 9front project continues an implementation of it.
content.origine_et_lignee_de_recherche_bell_labs:
Plan 9 originates in the Bell Labs research centre. The reference text, "Plan 9 from Bell Labs", is signed by Rob Pike, Dave Presotto, Sean Dorward, Bob Flandrena, Ken Thompson, Howard Trickey and Phil Winterbottom, all attached to the Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey. The authors place the genesis in the mid-1980s, in response to the trend that was then pushing users of large shared systems towards networks of personal machines: the overload of time-sharing machines and the desire for an environment controlled by the user led to the design of a system where the computing environment rebuilds itself on any machine of the network.

The text states that in 1989 the system was stable enough for some members of the team to use it as their exclusive computing environment. The fourth edition, documented by its release notes, dates from April 2002 and was updated in June 2003. These notes present it as a redesign of all levels: the 9P protocol, the kernel, the libraries and the applications. The 9P redesign responds to the impossibility of handling long file names; the new fossil file server supports them, while fs and kfs remain limited and are declared obsolete. The transition is ensured by lnfs, and the ramfs and u9fs servers work with long names.
content.depot_contrib_et_distribution_du_logicie:
Plan 9 does not rely on a central package manager comparable to those of Linux distributions. Complementary software is gathered in a tree called contrib, whose index is published on the project site. This index explicitly characterises its content: "Everything here is unsupported". Installing an entry is done with the command `contrib/install user/package`, which retrieves the tree deposited by an identified contributor; the contributor name and the package name make up the path.

The licence applicable to the elements of the tree is the Lucent Public License, unless otherwise stated in the entry itself. This organisation implies that the quality, maintenance and compatibility of an entry depend on its author: no central instance validates updates, signs archives or resolves dependencies. The base system, kernel, libraries and commands, is supplied with the distribution itself; additions go through contrib.

The pages consulted, the contrib index and the fourth edition notes, document neither a central binary repository, nor an apt- or rpm-type tool, nor a per-package version policy. This absence is recorded as a documentation limit: it does not allow the conclusion that the system has no distribution mechanism at all, only that the primary sources consulted describe none.
